title: Chapter 3: Synthesizable HDL Models of Sequential Circuits
text:
Learning objectives

Distinguish initial (single-pass) behavior from always (cyclic) behavior and know when each is used.
Generate a clock and control timing with the # delay and @ event operators.
Choose between blocking (=) and nonblocking (<=) assignments.
Model latches and flip-flops, including an asynchronous reset, in a form a synthesis tool can infer.
Model Mealy and Moore state machines from their state diagrams.
Describe a clocked sequential circuit structurally and verify it with a test bench.

title: Chapter 3: Synthesizable HDL Models of Sequential Circuits
text:
Overview

Behavioral models are abstract representations of the functionality of digital hardware. Designers write them to describe quickly how a circuit is to operate, without first specifying its hardware. This chapter continues the discussion of behavioral modeling from Chapter 2 and presents flip-flops and sequential circuits, in preparation for modeling more complex circuits.

title: Chapter 3: Synthesizable HDL Models of Sequential Circuits
text:
3.1 Behavioral Modeling

Two kinds of behavior
Verilog has two kinds of abstract behavior. Both begin executing when the simulator starts, at time t = 0.









initial
always




Name
Single-pass behavior
Cyclic behavior


What it contains
One statement, or a block of statements enclosed by begin … end or fork … join
Statements that are re-executed


Ends
Expires after its statement executes
Runs again and again until the simulation is stopped


Typical use
Stimulus signals in a test bench
Circuit behavior


Accepted by synthesis tools
No
Yes



A module can contain any number of initial or always statements. They execute concurrently with each other, starting at time 0, and can interact through shared variables.







ImportantImportant Note: Use initial for stimulus only



Designers use single-pass behavior primarily to describe stimulus signals in a test bench, never to model the behavior of a circuit.


A word description of a simple D flip-flop shows how always works: whenever the rising edge of the clock occurs, if the reset input is asserted, the output Q gets 0; otherwise Q gets the value of input D. The statements triggered by the clock repeat until the simulation ends. Section 3.2 shows this in Verilog.


Generating a clock
An initial statement runs once, starting at the beginning of simulation. It is useful for generating input signals. To simulate a sequential circuit you also need a clock source to trigger the flip-flops. Three ways to provide a free-running clock follow.
Version 1: a loop with repeat.


Clock from one initial block with repeat

Sets clock to 0, then repeats 30 times: wait 10 time units, complement clock.
initial begin
  clock = 1'b0;
  repeat (30) #10 clock = ~clock;
end

The initial block holds two statements inside begin and end. The first sets clock to 0 at time 0. The second is a loop that repeats 30 times, waiting 10 time units and then complementing clock. This produces 15 clock cycles, each with a cycle time of 20 time units.
Version 2: separate initial and always statements.


Clock from initial, a stopwatch, and always

Uses one initial to set the clock, a second initial to end the simulation, and an always statement as the clock generator.
initial begin
  clock = 1'b0;
end
initial #300 $finish;
always #10 clock = ~clock;


The first initial behavior has one statement: it sets clock to 0 at time 0 and then expires.
The second single-pass behavior is a stopwatch. The system task $finish ends the simulation unconditionally after 300 time units. With only one statement, begin … end is not needed.
After 10 time units, the always statement repeatedly complements clock, giving a clock generator with a cycle time of 20 time units.
The three behavioral statements can be written in any order.

Version 3: a forever loop.


Clock from a forever loop

Initializes clock, then complements it every 10 time units without end.
initial begin clock = 0; forever #10 clock = ~clock; end

This version initializes the clock and then executes an indefinite loop (forever) in which clock is complemented after a delay of 10 time steps. The single-pass behavior never finishes, so it does not expire; another behavior must terminate the simulation.


Timing and event control
The activity of either kind of behavior can be controlled by:

the delay operator #, which suspends execution until a specified time has elapsed. It is commonly used in single-pass behaviors, such as test-bench stimulus.
the event control operator @, which suspends activity until an event occurs. An event can be an unconditional change of a signal value (for example, @ A) or a specified transition of a signal value (for example, @ (posedge clock)).

The general form of an always statement with an event control expression is:


General form of an always block

Shows the template: an event control expression followed by procedural assignment statements in begin … end.
always @ (event control expression) begin
  // Procedural assignment statements that execute when the condition is met
end


The event control expression (also called the sensitivity list) is the condition that must occur to start executing the procedural statements.
The variables on the left-hand side of procedural statements must be of type reg and declared as such.
The right-hand side can be any expression built from Verilog operators.
Statements in the block execute sequentially, top to bottom. After the last one, the behavior waits for the event control expression to be satisfied again.

A sensitivity list can specify level-sensitive events, edge-sensitive events, or a combination of the two. Designers do not use the combination, because synthesis tools cannot translate it into hardware.

Level-sensitive events occur in combinational circuits and in latches. A change in A, B, or C starts an always block whose list contains those three signals.
Edge-sensitive events occur in synchronous sequential circuits, where flip-flops change only in response to a clock transition: a positive edge or a negative edge, but not both. Verilog provides the keywords posedge and negedge.

For example, a list containing posedge clock and negedge reset starts the block only if the clock makes a positive transition or reset makes a negative transition. Verilog 2001 and 2005 allow a comma-separated list.


Event control expressions

Shows three forms: a level-sensitive list (A or B or C), an edge-sensitive list with or (Verilog 1995), and the same list with a comma (Verilog 2001, 2005).
always @ (A or B or C)                       // level-sensitive
always @ (posedge clock or negedge reset)   // Verilog 1995
always @ (posedge clock, negedge reset)     // Verilog 2001, 2005





Verilog 1995
Verilog 2001, 2005




Separator in the event control expression
Keyword or
Comma





Procedural and continuous assignment
A procedural assignment assigns a logic value to a variable inside an initial or always statement. A continuous assignment (Chapter 2) is different:









Continuous assignment
Procedural assignment




Where
Outside behaviors, with assign
Inside initial or always


When it updates
Whenever a variable on its right-hand side changes (implicit level-sensitive list)
Only when the statement is executed



For example, the clock was complemented only when the statement clock = ~clock executed, which did not happen until 10 time units after the start of simulation. A reg variable keeps its value until a procedural assignment gives it a new one.


Blocking and nonblocking assignments
There are two kinds of procedural assignment, distinguished by their operator.









Blocking
Nonblocking




Operator
=
<=


Execution
Statements run sequentially, in the order listed
Right-hand sides of the whole set are evaluated first; left-hand sides are assigned afterward, together



Consider two procedural assignments, first as blocking:


Blocking assignments

Transfers A into B, then increments the new B and transfers it to C.
B = A;
C = B + 1;

The first statement transfers A into B. The second increments the new value of B and transfers it to C. When both finish, C contains A + 1.
Now the same two statements as nonblocking:


Nonblocking assignments

The same two assignments written with the nonblocking operator.
B <= A;
C <= B + 1;

The right-hand sides are evaluated and stored in temporary locations: the value of A in one, the value of B + 1 in another. Only after all the expressions in the block are evaluated are the left-hand sides assigned. Now C contains the original value of B, plus 1.






TipRemember: Which assignment to use




Use blocking assignments when sequential ordering is imperative, and in cyclic behavior that is level sensitive (combinational logic).
Use nonblocking assignments when modeling concurrent execution, for example edge-sensitive behavior such as synchronous, concurrent register transfers, and when modeling latched behavior.

Nonblocking assignments are imperative in register-transfer-level design: they model the concurrent operations of physical hardware synchronized by a common clock.


Today’s designers are expected to know which HDL features are useful in practice and how to avoid the ones that are not. Following these rules prevents conditions that lead synthesis tools astray and create mismatches between the behavior of a model and the behavior of the hardware that synthesis produces.

title: Chapter 3: Synthesizable HDL Models of Sequential Circuits
text:
Chapter Summary

initial runs once and is used for test-bench stimulus; always repeats and describes circuit behavior.
Use # for delays and @ (with posedge, negedge, or level changes) for event control.
Use blocking (=) for combinational logic and nonblocking (<=) for edge-sensitive and latched behavior.
Write an asynchronous reset so that the asynchronous tests come first in the if chain and the last else is the clock event; always include a reset.
A Mealy output depends on state and input and can glitch; a Moore output depends on state only.
A sequential circuit can be modeled behaviorally or structurally (T flip-flops plus combinational equations). Both versions synthesize to the same hardware.

title: Chapter 1: Hardware Description Language
text:
Learning objectives

Explain what a hardware description language (HDL) is and why circuits are simulated before they are built.
Name the main steps of an HDL-based design flow.
Read a basic Verilog module: keywords, identifiers, ports, wires, and gate instances.
Describe combinational logic with Boolean expressions.
Define a user-defined primitive (UDP) from a truth table.

title: Chapter 1: Hardware Description Language
text:
Chapter Overview


Why use an HDL?
Manual design methods work only for small circuits. Practical circuits are designed with computer-based tools. Combined with a correct-by-construction methodology, these tools make the most of the designer’s creativity and effort and reduce the risk of a flawed design.
Prototype integrated circuits are too expensive and slow to build. Modern design tools therefore rely on an HDL to describe, design, and test a circuit in software before it is manufactured.


What is an HDL?
A hardware description language (HDL) is a computer-based language that describes the hardware of digital systems in textual form. It resembles an ordinary programming language such as C, but it is oriented to hardware structures and the behavior of logic circuits.
An HDL can represent:

logic diagrams,
truth tables,
Boolean expressions, and
complex abstractions of the behavior of a digital system.

One useful view: an HDL describes the relationship between the signals that are inputs to a circuit and the signals that are its outputs. An HDL description of an AND gate, for example, describes how the gate’s output value is determined by the values of its inputs.
An HDL is also a documentation language. Its descriptions can be read by both humans and computers, serve as an exchange language between designers, and can be stored, retrieved, edited, transmitted, and processed by software efficiently.


Where HDLs are used in the design flow
HDLs are used in several major steps of integrated-circuit design:







Step
What it does




Design entry
Creates an HDL description of the functionality to be implemented in hardware.


Functional simulation (verification)
Shows how the described circuit behaves, before it is fabricated.


Logic synthesis
Derives a netlist of physical components and interconnections from the HDL model.


Timing verification
Confirms that the fabricated circuit will run at the specified speed.


Fault simulation
Finds input patterns that tell a faulty circuit from a fault-free one.



Design entry. Depending on the HDL, the description can take several forms: Boolean logic equations, truth tables, a netlist of interconnected gates, or an abstract behavioral model. An HDL model may also represent one partition of a larger circuit, divided into smaller interconnected and interacting functional units.
Logic simulation. A simulator interprets the HDL description and either produces readable output (such as a time-ordered sequence of input and output values) or displays waveforms. Simulation detects functional errors without physically building and operating the circuit. Errors are corrected by modifying the HDL statements.






NoteKey Concept: Test bench



The stimulus (the logic values applied to a circuit’s inputs) that tests the functionality of a design is called a test bench. A test bench is also written in the HDL.
To simulate a digital system, first describe the design in an HDL, then verify it by simulating it and checking it with a test bench. Formal mathematical methods can prove that a circuit is correct, but they are more complex; this course focuses on simulation.


Logic synthesis. Synthesis derives a list of physical components and their interconnections, called a netlist, from the HDL model. The netlist can be used to fabricate an integrated circuit or to lay out a printed circuit board.

Synthesis is similar to compiling a program in a high-level language, except that it produces a database describing the elements and structure of a circuit instead of object code.
It is based on formal, exact procedures and covers the part of digital design that can be automated.
Today’s large, complex circuits are possible because of logic synthesis software.

Timing verification. Every logic gate has a propagation delay, so a change at a circuit’s input cannot instantly change its output. Propagation delays limit how fast a circuit can operate. Timing verification checks each signal path against these delays. It runs after synthesis has specified the actual devices and before the circuit is released for production.
Fault simulation. In VLSI design, fault simulation compares the behavior of an ideal circuit with that of a circuit containing a process-induced flaw (for example, dust or other particles in the clean room). It identifies input stimuli, called test patterns, that reveal the difference. These patterns are used to test fabricated devices so only good devices ship. Test generation and fault simulation may happen at different steps, but always before production, so the circuit’s internal logic can be tested.


Why Verilog?
Two HDLs are public standards supported by the IEEE: VHDL and Verilog.

VHDL was mandated by the U.S. Department of Defense. The V stands for VHSIC, an acronym for very high speed integrated circuit.
Verilog began as a proprietary HDL of Cadence Design Systems. Cadence transferred control to Open Verilog International (OVI), a consortium of companies and universities, as a step toward IEEE standardization.

VHDL is more difficult to learn. Verilog is easier to describe, learn, and use, so it is the language of this course.
The Verilog examples also introduce a general design methodology: computer-aided modeling of digital systems with a typical HDL. The emphasis is on modeling, verification, and synthesis (both manual and automated) of Verilog models of circuits with specified behavior.
Verilog was first approved as a standard HDL in 1995; revised versions were approved in 2001 and 2005. The course covers only the Verilog features, including those in the latest standard, that support HDL-based design of integrated circuits.

title: Chapter 1: Hardware Description Language
text:
1.1 Module Declaration

Basic language rules
The Verilog language reference manual defines precisely which constructs are legal. A Verilog model is written with keywords, of which there are about 100. Keywords are predefined, lowercase identifiers that define language constructs. Examples: module, endmodule, input, output, wire, and, or, not.


Comments. Text from // to the end of the line is a comment. Multiline comments begin with /* and end with */. Comments have no effect on simulation.
White space is ignored, but it may not appear inside a keyword, a user-defined identifier, an operator, or a number.
Case sensitivity. Uppercase and lowercase letters are different (not is not the same as NOT).
Keywords in this handbook. They are highlighted in code examples for clarity; highlighting is not a language requirement.

A module is the text enclosed by the keyword pair module … endmodule. It is the fundamental descriptive unit of Verilog: it is declared with module and must always end with endmodule.
Combinational logic can be described by a schematic connection of gates, a set of Boolean equations, or a truth table. Verilog supports all three styles. We start with a gate-level description of the circuit in Figure 3.37.




Figure 3.37. Circuit to demonstrate an HDL





Reading the first example


HDL Example 3.1 Combinational logic modeled with primitives

Describes the circuit of Figure 3.37 as a module that instantiates three primitive gates.
// HDL Example 3.1 (combinational logic modeled with primitives)
module Simple_Circuit (A, B, C, D, E);
  output D, E;
  input  A, B, C;
  wire   w1;

  and G1 (w1, A, B);   // Optional gate instance name
  not G2 (E, C);
  or  G3 (D, w1, E);
endmodule

The example has the following parts, in order:

An optional comment line that helps the reader.
The module line, which starts the declaration. module is followed by a name and a port list.
Direction declarations (input, output) saying which ports are inputs and which are outputs.
A wire declaration for each internal connection. This circuit has one: the connection w1.
Gate instantiations that give the structure of the circuit.
endmodule.

Identifiers are names given to modules, variables (such as signals), and other language elements so they can be referenced in the design. The module in this example is named Simple_Circuit. Choose meaningful names. Identifiers:

are made of alphanumeric characters and the underscore (_),
are case sensitive,
must start with a letter or an underscore, and
cannot start with a digit.

Port list. The ports are the interface between the module and its environment. Here they are the circuit’s inputs and outputs. The environment sets the input values; the outputs are determined inside the circuit by the action of the inputs. The list is enclosed in parentheses, its elements are separated by commas, and the statement ends with a semicolon (;).
Gate instances. The structure of the circuit is a list of predefined primitive gates (and, not, or). Each listing is a gate instantiation, and each resulting gate is a gate instance. An instantiation has:

an optional instance name (G1, G2, …),
followed by the gate output and inputs, separated by commas and enclosed in parentheses.

For example, the OR gate of the schematic is the or primitive named G3, with output D and inputs w1 and E.






ImportantImportant Note: Port order and semicolons




The output of a primitive is always listed first, followed by its inputs. (The ports of a module may be listed in any order.)
Every statement ends with a semicolon, but there is no semicolon after endmodule.









NoteKey Concept: Declaration versus instantiation



A Verilog module is declared. Its declaration specifies the input-output behavior of the hardware it represents.
Predefined primitives are not declared, because the language defines them and users cannot change them. Primitives are instantiated (used), just as gates are used to populate a printed circuit board. Once a module has been declared, it can also be instantiated inside other designs.








TipRemember: A Verilog model describes, it does not compute



Simple_Circuit is not a computational model like a program in an ordinary language. The order of its statements does not specify a sequence of computation. The model states which primitives form the circuit and how they are connected. Because the behavior of every gate is defined, the input-output behavior follows implicitly, and the model can be simulated.

title: Chapter 1: Hardware Description Language
text:
1.2 Boolean Expressions
Boolean equations describing combinational logic are written in Verilog as a continuous assignment: the keyword assign followed by a Boolean expression.
Verilog uses these symbols so logical operators are distinct from arithmetic operators:



Symbol
Logic operation




&
AND


|
OR


~
NOT (complement)



The circuit of Figure 3.37 can be written with a single Boolean expression:


Figure 3.37 as a Boolean expression

Shows one assign statement that describes the same circuit as Example 3.1.
assign D = (A & B) | ~C;

The next example describes a circuit with two outputs, specified by these Boolean equations:

E = A + BC + B’D
F = B’C + BC’D’



HDL Example 3.4 Combinational circuit modeled with Boolean equations

Uses two assign statements to define outputs E and F from inputs A, B, C, and D.
// HDL Example 3.4 (combinational logic modeled with Boolean equations)
module Circuit_Boolean_CA (E, F, A, B, C, D);
  output E, F;
  input  A, B, C, D;

  assign E = A | (B & C) | (~B & D);
  assign F = (~B & C) | (B & ~C & ~D);
endmodule

The circuit has four inputs (A, B, C, D) and two outputs (E, F). The two assign statements describe the Boolean equations. During simulation, the values of E and F are determined dynamically by the values of A, B, C, and D: when the test bench changes one or more inputs, the simulator updates E and F.






NoteKey Concept: Continuous assignment



The assignment is called continuous because the relationship between the assigned value and the variable is permanent. A continuous assignment behaves like combinational logic and has a gate-level equivalent circuit. It is also called implicit combinational logic.


So far, a digital circuit has been described with HDL statements, a circuit diagram, and a Boolean expression. A third alternative is a truth table, covered next.

title: Chapter 1: Hardware Description Language
Chapter 1: Hardware Description Language
text:
Chapter Summary

An HDL describes digital hardware as text and supports design entry, simulation, synthesis, timing verification, and fault simulation.
A test bench supplies the input stimulus for simulation and is itself written in the HDL.
A Verilog module (module … endmodule) has a name, a port list, direction declarations, internal wires, and gate or other statements.
Primitives are instantiated; modules are declared. The output of a primitive is listed first.
Boolean equations use assign with &, |, ~, and the assignment stays active for the whole simulation.
A UDP describes a circuit by a truth table inside primitive … endprimitive.

Next: Chapter 2 compares gate-level, dataflow, and behavioral models of combinational circuits.

text:
How to read this handbook







Element
What it tells you




Key Concept
A definition or idea you need before moving on.


Remember
A rule of thumb to keep in mind while coding.


Important Note
A rule or restriction that causes errors if ignored.


Technical Detail
Extra precision for readers who want the full picture.


Example
A numbered HDL example, shown with a copyable code block.



Code blocks have a copy button in the top-right corner. Figures keep their original numbers (for example, Figure 3.37), so you can match them to your lecture notes. Use the search box in the top bar to find any keyword.

title: Chapter 2: HDL Models of Combinational Circuits
text:
Learning objectives

Compare the three modeling styles for combinational logic: gate-level, dataflow, and behavioral.
Use the four-valued logic system (0, 1, x, z) and read the primitive-gate truth tables.
Build a hierarchical design by instantiating modules inside other modules.
Model three-state gates and shared (multiple-driver) nets.
Write continuous assignments with Verilog operators, including concatenation and the conditional operator.
Write simple behavioral models with always, if-else, and case.

title: Chapter 2: HDL Models of Combinational Circuits
text:
Modeling styles

The module is the basic building block for modeling hardware in Verilog. The logic of a module can be described in any one of the following styles, or in a combination of them:








Style
Describes the circuit with
Keyword




Gate-level
Instances of predefined and user-defined primitive gates, and how they connect
gate names such as and, or


Dataflow
Continuous assignment statements, mostly Boolean equations
assign


Behavioral
Procedural assignment statements, at a higher level of abstraction
always



Behavioral modeling can describe both combinational and sequential circuits. A fourth style, switch-level modeling, is sometimes used to simulate MOS transistor circuits but not for logic synthesis; it is outside the scope of this chapter. Sequential circuits are presented in Chapter 3.

title: Chapter 2: HDL Models of Combinational Circuits
text:
2.1 Gate-level Modeling
Gate-level modeling gives a textual description of a schematic diagram: the circuit is specified by its logic gates and their interconnections.

Primitive gates
Verilog includes 12 basic gates as predefined primitives:

Eight ordinary gates: and, nand, or, nor, xor, xnor, not, buf.
Four three-state gates (see 2.2).

All are written with lowercase keywords. The gates and, nand, or, nor, xor, and xnor are n-input primitives: they can have any number of scalar inputs (for example, a three-input and). The buf and not primitives are n-output primitives: a single input can drive several output lines, each with its own identifier.


Four-valued logic
Each gate has a functional description based on a four-valued system. At any instant, the simulator assigns one of these values to a gate output:



Value
Meaning




0
Logic 0


1
Logic 1


x
Unknown


z
High impedance




An unknown value (x) is assigned when a signal’s value is ambiguous, for example when it cannot be determined whether it is 0 or 1 (such as a flip-flop without a reset condition).
A high-impedance value (z) occurs at the output of a three-state gate that is not enabled, or on a wire that was left unconnected by mistake.

TipRemember: Reading the AND and OR tables




AND: the output is 1 only when both inputs are 1. It is 0 if any input is 0. Otherwise (an input is x or z), it is x.
OR: the output is 0 only when both inputs are 0. It is 1 if any input is 1. Otherwise, it is x.





Instantiating primitives
When a primitive gate is listed in a module, it is instantiated in that module. In general, component instantiations are statements that reference lower-level components, creating unique copies (instances) of them in the higher-level module. Think of instantiation as the HDL counterpart of placing and connecting parts on a circuit board.


Vectors
Identifiers with several bits are called vectors. A vector is declared with a range in square brackets: two numbers separated by a colon.


Vector declarations

Declares a four-bit output vector D (bits 0 through 3) and an eight-bit wire vector SUM (bits 7 through 0).
output [0:3] D;
wire [7:0] SUM;


The leftmost number in the range is always the most significant bit of the vector.
A single bit is selected with square brackets: D[2] is bit 2 of D.
A contiguous part of a vector can be selected too: SUM[2:0] is the three least significant bits of SUM.



Example: two-to-four-line decoder
Figure 4.19 shows the circuit modeled in Example 4.1.




Figure 4.19. Two-to-four-line decoder with enable input





HDL Example 4.1 Gate-level two-to-four-line decoder

Uses three not gates and four nand gates to build a decoder with data inputs A and B, an enable input, and a four-bit output vector D.
// HDL Example 4.1
// Gate-level description of two-to-four-line decoder
// Refer to Fig. 4.19 with symbol E replaced by enable, for clarity.
module decoder_2x4_gates (D, A, B, enable);
  output [0:3] D;
  input        A, B;
  input        enable;
  wire         A_not, B_not, enable_not;

  not
    G1 (A_not, A),
    G2 (B_not, B),
    G3 (enable_not, enable);
  nand
    G4 (D[0], A_not, B_not, enable_not),
    G5 (D[1], A_not, B,     enable_not),
    G6 (D[2], A,     B_not, enable_not),
    G7 (D[3], A,     B,     enable_not);
endmodule

The decoder has two data inputs, A and B, and an enable input. The four outputs form the vector D. Internal connections are declared as wires. Three not gates produce the complements of the inputs, and four nand gates produce the outputs.






ImportantImportant Note: Listing several gates of one type



The keywords not and nand are written once and are not repeated for each gate. Put a comma at the end of each gate in the series and end the last one with a semicolon. Remember that the output is always listed first in a primitive’s port list.




Hierarchical design: ripple-carry adder
Two or more modules can be combined into a hierarchical description. There are two basic design methodologies:







Methodology
Order of work




Top-down
Define the top-level block first, then identify the sub-blocks needed to build it.


Bottom-up
Identify the building blocks first, then combine them into the top-level block.



Consider the four-bit binary adder. It is a top-level block built from four full adders, and each full adder is built from two half adders (plus some glue logic). A top-down design defines the four-bit adder first, then the full adders, then the half adders. A bottom-up design defines the half adder first, then the full adder, then the four-bit adder.
HDL Example 4.2 is a bottom-up description:

The half adder is defined by instantiating primitive gates.
The full adder instantiates two half adders.
The four-bit adder instantiates four full adders.

Figures 4.5, 4.8, and 4.9 show these three levels of the design.




Figure 4.5. Implementation of half adder







Figure 4.8. Implementation of full adder with two half adders and an OR gate







Figure 4.9. Four-bit adder





HDL Example 4.2 Gate-level four-bit ripple-carry adder

Builds the adder bottom-up from three modules: a half adder, a full adder, and the four-bit ripple-carry adder.
Module half_adder
// HDL Example 4.2
// Gate-level description of four-bit ripple carry adder
// Description of half adder (Fig. 4.5b)
// Verilog 1995 syntax:
//   module half_adder (S, C, x, y);
//   output S, C;
//   input  x, y;
// Verilog 2001, 2005 syntax:
module half_adder (output S, C, input x, y);
  // Instantiate primitive gates
  xor (S, x, y);
  and (C, x, y);
endmodule
Module full_adder
// Description of full adder (Fig. 4.8)
// Verilog 1995 syntax:
//   module full_adder (S, C, x, y, z);
//   output S, C;
//   input  x, y, z;
// Verilog 2001, 2005 syntax:
module full_adder (output S, C, input x, y, z);
  wire S1, C1, C2;

  // Instantiate half adders
  half_adder HA1 (S1, C1, x, y);
  half_adder HA2 (S, C2, S1, z);
  or         G1  (C, C2, C1);
endmodule
Four-bit ripple-carry adder module
// Description of four-bit adder (Fig. 4.9)
// Verilog 1995 syntax:
//   module ripple_carry_4_bit_adder (Sum, C4, A, B, C0);
//   output [3:0] Sum;
//   output       C4;
//   input  [3:0] A, B;
//   input        C0;
// Alternative Verilog 2001, 2005 syntax:
module ripple_carry_4_bit_adder (output [3:0] Sum, output C4, input [3:0] A, B, input C0);
  wire C1, C2, C3;   // Intermediate carries

  // Instantiate chain of full adders
  full_adder FA0 (Sum[0], C1, A[0], B[0], C0),
             FA1 (Sum[1], C2, A[1], B[1], C1),
             FA2 (Sum[2], C3, A[2], B[2], C2),
             FA3 (Sum[3], C4, A[3], B[3], C3);
endmodule

Instantiation syntax. A module is instantiated by writing the name of the module followed by an instance name and a (new or the same) set of port names. For example, the half adder instance HA1 inside the full adder is connected to S1, C1, x, and y, which produces a half adder with outputs S1 and C1 and inputs x and y.
Identifier rule. The first character of an identifier cannot be a digit, but it can be an underscore, so the module name _4bitadder is valid. A meaningful alternative that needs no leading underscore is adder_4_bit.
Port-declaration syntax. Example 4.2 uses the Verilog 2001/2005 style, which declares the port mode (output), type (reg), and vector range ([3:0]) in the module header. The 1995 standard uses separate statements for these.









Verilog 1995
Verilog 2001, 2005




Port declarations
Separate input / output statements after the module header
Mode, type, and range inside the header’s port list


Typing effort
More
Less (no repeated identifiers)









ImportantImportant Note: Nesting rules




Modules can be instantiated (nested) inside other modules.
Module declarations cannot be nested: a module … endmodule definition cannot be placed between the module and endmodule keywords of another module. The only way to use one module inside another is to instantiate it.
Instance names are required when instantiating modules (such as FA0), but optional for primitive gates.









NoteKey Concept: Structural description and hierarchy



A module is a structural description if it is composed of instantiations of other modules. Instantiating modules within other modules creates a hierarchical decomposition of the design.
In the adder, the top level (parent) is the four-bit adder. The four full adders are its child modules, and so on. C0 is an input of the cell forming the least significant bit of the chain; C4 is the output of the cell forming the most significant bit.

title: Chapter 2: HDL Models of Combinational Circuits
text:
2.2 Three-State Gates
A three-state gate has a control input that can place the gate in a high-impedance state, written z in Verilog. There are four types, shown in Figure 4.31.




Figure 4.31. Three-state gates












Gate
Control value that enables it
Output when enabled
Output when not enabled




bufif1
1
input (like a normal buffer)
z


bufif0
0
input (like a normal buffer)
z


notif1
1
complement of the input
z


notif0
0
complement of the input
z



Three-state gates are instantiated with the form gate name (output, input, control). In simulation the output can be 0, 1, x, or z.


Three-state gate instantiations

Shows one bufif1 instance and one notif0 instance.
bufif1 (OUT, A, control);
notif0 (Y, B, enable);


In the first instance, input A is transferred to OUT when control = 1; OUT goes to z when control = 0.
In the second instance, output Y = z when enable = 1, and Y = B' (the complement of B) when enable = 0.


Several drivers on one line
The outputs of several three-state gates can be tied together to form a common output line. To mark such a connection, Verilog uses the keyword tri (for tri-state), which indicates that the net has multiple drivers. Figure 4.32 is a two-to-one-line multiplexer built from three-state buffers; its output must be declared with the tri data type.




Figure 4.32. Two-to-one-line multiplexer with three-state buffers





Multiplexer with three-state output

Describes the multiplexer of Figure 4.32 with a bufif1 and a bufif0 driving the same tri output.
// Mux with three-state output
module mux_tri (m_out, A, B, select);
  output m_out;
  input A, B, select;
  tri m_out;
  bufif1 (m_out, A, select);
  bufif0 (m_out, B, select);
endmodule

The two three-state buffers drive the same output. To show that they share one connection, m_out must be declared with the keyword tri.


Nets
wire and tri are examples of a class of data types called nets, which represent connections between hardware elements. In simulation, a net’s value is determined by a continuous assignment or by the device whose output it represents. The word net is not a keyword; it names the class.



Net type
Models




wire
An ordinary connection. The most frequently used net.


tri
A connection with multiple three-state drivers.


wor
The wired-OR configuration (emitter-coupled logic).


wand
The wired-AND configuration (open-collector technology).


supply1
Power supply; hardwires an input to 1.


supply0
Ground; hardwires an input to 0.



According to the language rules, an identifier that is used but not declared is interpreted by default as a wire.

title: Chapter 2: HDL Models of Combinational Circuits
text:
2.3 Dataflow Modeling
Dataflow modeling describes combinational logic with operators that act on operands. Verilog provides about 30 operators; Table 4.10 lists some of them. (The complete list for Verilog 2001 and 2005 is in Table 8.1, Section 8.2.)


Table 4.10: Some Verilog HDL Operators






Symbol
Operation




+
Binary addition


-
Binary subtraction


&
Bitwise AND


|
Bitwise OR


^
Bitwise XOR


~
Bitwise NOT


==
Equality


>
Greater than


<
Less than


{ }
Concatenation


?:
Conditional





Notes on the operators:

Arithmetic and logic operations use different symbols: + is arithmetic addition, while & is the bitwise logic AND. There are separate symbols for bitwise OR, NOT, and XOR.
The equality operator uses two equals signs (==, with no space between them) to distinguish it from the single = used in the assign statement.
Bitwise operators work bit by bit on a pair of vector operands.
Concatenation appends several operands. For example, two 2-bit operands can be concatenated into one 4-bit operand.
The conditional operator acts like a multiplexer (see Example 4.6 below).


Continuous assignments and nets
Dataflow modeling uses continuous assignments and the keyword assign. A continuous assignment assigns a value to a net. The net data types represent a physical connection between circuit elements.

A net is declared explicitly with a net keyword (for example, wire) or by declaring an identifier to be an output port.
The logic value of a net is determined by what the net is connected to. If it is connected to a gate output, the net is said to be driven by the gate, and its value follows from the gate’s input values and truth table.
If the net is the left-hand side of a continuous assignment, its value is given by an expression made of operands and operators.


For example, a two-line multiplexer with data inputs A and B, select input S, and output Y can be described with one continuous assignment (assuming the variables were declared):


Multiplexer as one continuous assignment

Relates output Y to inputs A, B, and S with one assign statement and a Boolean expression.
assign Y = (A & S) | (B & ~S);

The relationship between Y, A, B, and S is declared by assign, followed by the target output Y, an equals sign, and a Boolean expression. In hardware terms, the assignment is equivalent to connecting the output of the OR gate to wire Y.


Dataflow versions of earlier examples
The next two examples are dataflow models of the two earlier gate-level examples.


HDL Example 4.3 Dataflow two-to-four-line decoder

Uses four continuous assignment statements with Boolean expressions, one per output.
// HDL Example 4.3
// Dataflow description of two-to-four-line decoder
// See Fig. 4.19. Note: The figure uses symbol E, but the
// Verilog model uses enable to clearly indicate functionality.
module decoder_2x4_df (   // Verilog 2001, 2005 syntax
  output [0:3] D,
  input        A, B, enable
);
  assign D[0] = ~(~A & ~B & ~enable),
         D[1] = ~(~A &  B & ~enable),
         D[2] = ~( A & ~B & ~enable),
         D[3] = ~( A &  B & ~enable);
endmodule



HDL Example 4.4 Dataflow four-bit adder

Describes the whole adder with one statement that combines addition and concatenation.
// HDL Example 4.4
// Dataflow description of four-bit adder
// Verilog 2001, 2005 module port syntax
module binary_adder (
  output [3:0] Sum,
  output       C_out,
  input  [3:0] A, B,
  input        C_in
);
  assign {C_out, Sum} = A + B + C_in;
endmodule

In Example 4.4, the plus symbol (+) adds the four bits of A, the four bits of B, and the one bit C_in. The target is the concatenation of the output carry C_out and the four bits of Sum. Concatenation is written inside braces with commas between the operands, so {C_out, Sum} is the five-bit result of the addition.


Comparator and multiplexer
Dataflow models describe circuits by their function rather than by their gate structure. This makes design easier, as the comparator shows.


HDL Example 4.5 Dataflow four-bit magnitude comparator

Defines three outputs (less than, greater than, equal) from two four-bit inputs using comparison operators.
// HDL Example 4.5
// Dataflow description of a four-bit comparator
module mag_compare (output A_lt_B, A_eq_B, A_gt_B, input [3:0] A, B);
  assign A_lt_B = (A < B);
  assign A_gt_B = (A > B);
  assign A_eq_B = (A == B);
endmodule

The module has two 4-bit inputs, A and B, and three outputs:

A_lt_B is 1 if A is less than B,
A_gt_B is 1 if A is greater than B,
A_eq_B is 1 if A is equal to B.

Equality is written with two equals signs (==) to distinguish it from the assignment operator (=). A Verilog synthesis compiler can accept this module as input, run synthesis algorithms, and produce a netlist and a schematic of an equivalent circuit without manual intervention.






NoteKey Concept: The conditional operator



The conditional operator ? : takes three operands: condition ? true-expression : false-expression.
The condition is evaluated. If the result is logic 1, the true expression is evaluated; if it is logic 0, the false expression is evaluated. Together they are equivalent to an if-else condition.




HDL Example 4.6 Dataflow two-to-one-line multiplexer

Uses the conditional operator in a continuous assignment: the output is A if select = 1, otherwise B.
// HDL Example 4.6
// Dataflow description of two-to-one-line multiplexer
module mux_2x1_df (m_out, A, B, select);
  output m_out;
  input  A, B;
  input  select;

  assign m_out = (select) ? A : B;
endmodule

title: Chapter 2: HDL Models of Combinational Circuits
text:
2.4 Behavioral Modeling
Behavioral modeling represents digital circuits at a functional and algorithmic level. It is used mostly to describe sequential circuits but can also describe combinational ones. Two simple combinational examples introduce it here; behavioral modeling is covered in more detail in Chapter 3, after the study of sequential circuits.
A behavioral description uses the keyword always, followed by an optional event control expression and a list of procedural assignment statements. The event control expression says when the statements execute.






ImportantImportant Note: Targets must be reg



The target of a procedural assignment must be of the reg data type. A reg keeps its value until a new value is assigned to it (in contrast to a net, which is continuously driven).



Two-to-one-line multiplexer


HDL Example 4.7 Behavioral two-to-one-line multiplexer

Uses an always block with an if-else statement (compare with Example 4.6).
// HDL Example 4.7
// Behavioral description of two-to-one-line multiplexer
module mux_2x1_beh (m_out, A, B, select);
  output m_out;
  input  A, B, select;
  reg    m_out;

  always @(A or B or select)
    if (select == 1) m_out = A;
    else             m_out = B;
endmodule


Because m_out is a target output, it must be declared as reg, in addition to its output declaration.
The statements in the always block run every time any variable listed after the @ symbol changes: here A, B, or select.
There is no semicolon at the end of the always statement.
The keyword or (not the bitwise operator |) separates the variables in the list.
The if-else statement chooses based on the value of select.

The if statement can be written without the equality symbol; this form checks whether select is logic 1:


Shorthand if test

Shows an if that tests select for logic 1 without writing == 1.
if (select) m_out = A;



Four-to-one-line multiplexer


HDL Example 4.8 Behavioral four-to-one-line multiplexer

Uses a case statement on a two-bit select vector to choose one of four inputs.
// HDL Example 4.8
// Behavioral description of four-to-one-line multiplexer
// Verilog 2001, 2005 port syntax
module mux_4x1_beh (output reg m_out, input in_0, in_1, in_2, in_3, input [1:0] select);
  always @(in_0, in_1, in_2, in_3, select)   // Verilog 2001, 2005 syntax
    case (select)
      2'b00: m_out = in_0;
      2'b01: m_out = in_1;
      2'b10: m_out = in_2;
      2'b11: m_out = in_3;
    endcase
endmodule

The select input is a two-bit vector and the output is declared reg. The always statement contains a sequential block enclosed by case and endcase. The block runs whenever any input in the list changes value.
case is a multiway conditional branch. When an input or select changes:

The case expression (select) is evaluated.
Its value is compared, from top to bottom, with the case items.
The statement of the first matching case item is executed.
If there is no match, no statement is executed.

select is a two-bit number, so it can be 00, 01, 10, or 11. The case items have an implied priority because the list is evaluated from top to bottom.






NoteKey Concept: Sensitivity list



The list after the @ symbol is called a sensitivity list (Verilog 2001, 2005). It is equivalent to the event control expression of Verilog 1995, formed by “ORing” the signals.



Verilog 1995
Verilog 2001, 2005




Signals separated by the keyword or
Signals separated by commas







Implicit sensitivity list
A sensitivity list is only useful if it is complete, and in a large design it is easy to forget a signal. Verilog 2001 therefore lets you write @* or @(*) without a list: the block is then sensitive to every variable referenced on the right-hand side of its assignments.


Two forms of always without a list

Two equivalent ways to write it; in both, the block is sensitive to a and b without listing them.
always @*        // sensitive to every variable read on the right-hand side
  y = a & b;

always @(*)      // same meaning, parenthesized form
  y = a & b;







ImportantImportant Note: Incomplete lists create latches



A level-sensitive always block that describes combinational logic must list every variable referenced on the right-hand side of its assignments. If the list is incomplete, the logic is synthesized with latches at its outputs. This wastes silicon area, and the synthesized circuit may no longer match the simulation of the model.








TipRemember: @* for combinational logic



With @*, the block is interpreted and synthesized as level-sensitive combinational logic whose implicit sensitivity list contains every referenced variable. This prevents accidental latches.




Writing numbers
Binary numbers are written with the letter b preceded by a prime (apostrophe). The size is written first, then the value. For example, 2'b01 is a two-bit binary number with value 01.



Letter
Base




b
Binary


d
Decimal


o
Octal


h
Hexadecimal




Numbers are stored as bit patterns, but they can be written in any of these bases.
If the base is not specified, the number is decimal.
If the size is not specified, the system assumes at least 32 bits (more if the host simulator has a longer word, such as 64 bits).
The integer data type is stored in a 32-bit representation.
An underscore may be inserted in a number to improve readability, for example 16'b0101_1110_0101_0011. It has no other effect.




casex, casez, and default
The case construct has two variations:







Construct
Treated as don’t-cares when matching




casex
Any bit of the case expression or case item that is x or z


casez
Only bits that are z



If the case items do not cover all bit patterns of the case expression, some patterns have no match. Unlisted patterns can be handled with the default keyword as the last case item; its statement runs when no other item matches.






TipRemember: Why default matters



default is useful when a sequential machine has more possible state codes than are actually used. It lets the designer map all unused states to a chosen next state without elaborating each one, rather than letting the synthesis tool assign the next state arbitrarily.


The behavioral examples here are simple. Behavioral modeling and procedural assignment statements require knowledge of sequential circuits, which Chapter 3 covers next.

title: Chapter 2: HDL Models of Combinational Circuits
text:
Chapter Summary

Combinational logic can be modeled at gate level (and, or, … instances), as dataflow (assign), or behaviorally (always).
Verilog uses four logic values: 0, 1, x (unknown), and z (high impedance).
Modules are combined hierarchically by instantiation; module declarations cannot be nested.
Three-state gates (bufif1, bufif0, notif1, notif0) output z when disabled; nets with several drivers use tri.
Dataflow models use operators, concatenation { }, and the conditional operator ? :.
Behavioral models use always with reg targets, if-else, and case (with default, casex, and casez). Writing always @* makes the sensitivity list complete and avoids accidental latches.
